criteria.note: The single most-needed phrase, its translation, and the show-don't-say instruction all land inside the first ~150 words, which is exactly the intent behind 'korean gluten free phrases'.
Title renders at 53 chars including the appended suffix, description at ~135 chars, keyword carried in the title, and the description adds distinct information rather than repeating it.
Headings are argumentative rather than labelling, and a skim of headings alone reconstructs the whole thesis.
Five internal links each placed where the reader has just hit the limit of what this page can answer.
All five frontmatter Q/As trace to visible body text, including the wheat-flour caveat, the no-pronunciation policy, and the labelling spelling note.
Concrete but thin on checkable particulars: the strongest anecdote has a quantity but no venue, dish, or month.
criteria.evidence_quote: during our first year back in Korea (2025–26), one bakery owner told us — cheerfully, without being pressed — that his was 10% wheat

criteria.note: Korean terms are glossed precisely, a named product and a numbered MFDS notice are given, and the absence of romanisation is an explained editorial choice rather than vagueness.
Both external claims are anchored to primary sources with dates — Sempio's own product page and the MFDS labelling standard with its notice number and date.
The piece repeatedly states what its method cannot establish, offers an independent verification route, and carries no commercial or affiliate links to disclose.

findings.quote: one bakery owner told us — cheerfully, without being pressed — that his was 10% wheat
findings.why: This is the only fully concrete first-hand incident in the piece, and it carries no venue, neighbourhood, or month — so a reader has nothing to weigh it against, and the experience signal reads as recalled impression rather than observed fact.
findings.fix: Name the bakery (or at minimum the neighbourhood and month), and add one comparable dated instance for the BBQ grill-plate ask and the 간장 question. One named place with a date does more for this criterion than three unattributed impressions.

findings.quote: It comes from our own eating between 2025 and 2026, as a couple with one gluten-free person, across Seoul, Gyeonggi and Cheonan
findings.why: The honest 'we didn't count' framing is good for trust, but here it currently stands in place of the observed detail rather than accompanying it — the reader gets the caveat without the underlying incident.
findings.fix: Pair the caveat with at least one dated, located example where 글루텐프리 visibly failed and 알러지 worked: the restaurant, what was ordered, what the server did before and after the wording changed.

findings.quote: The literal translation is 글루텐프리, and it is the phrase least likely to get you a useful answer.
findings.why: FAQ answer 1 runs well past the length Google renders in a rich result and buries the 간장 caveat at the very end, so the part most likely to be truncated is the part a coeliac reader most needs.
findings.fix: Trim to roughly two sentences with the actionable phrase first, and split the wheat-flour-versus-wheat-grain caveat into its own short FAQ so neither gets cut.

findings.quote: We have not checked individual bottles on Korean shelves against that definition
findings.why: This kind of limit-setting is the strongest trust signal in the piece, but most of it sits in the final section, after the point where many readers will have copied the phrase block and left.
findings.fix: Surface a one-line 'what this guide is and isn't' note near the top so the scope disclosure reaches readers who never reach 'What these phrases can't do'.

criteria.note: Nearly every claim is either sourced (Sempio, MFDS) or explicitly marked as the authors' own unmeasured observation, but one behavioural generalisation about Korean service culture is asserted flatly with no attribution — it does not drive a safety decision.
criteria.evidence_quote: Korean service culture is accommodating, and a specific, apologetic ask is usually met well.

criteria.note: Product name (Sempio 501), the MFDS notice number and date, and the observation window (2025–26) are all concrete, linked, and mutually consistent; no invented statistic appears anywhere — the article explicitly refuses to invent a prevalence figure.

The article repeatedly states how it knows what it knows and what that cannot establish — 'we did not count conversations or record outcomes', 'a shopping habit, not a survey of the category', 'We have not checked individual bottles' — and never dresses anecdote up as analysis.

No absolute safety claim anywhere; cross-contamination (fryer, grill plate, pan, tongs) is given its own phrases and its own limits section, and the authors explicitly separate their NCGS household from coeliac requirements rather than conflating them.
Both external sources carry retrieval dates (August 2026) and the MFDS notice carries its own issue date, and reformulation staleness is flagged directly for products.

Every Korean line is idiomatic and correctly glossed, the 알러지/알레르기 and 알레르기 유발물질 distinction is right, the 양조/조선/혼합간장 categories are described correctly, and the load-bearing labelling fact — wheat mandatory, barley and rye not — is stated accurately.
The reader is given a concrete self-check path (read 원재료명 with the four-word scan, phone ahead using the same phrases) and is told plainly it 'doesn't require trusting us or the staff'.

findings.quote: Korean service culture is accommodating, and a specific, apologetic ask is usually met well.
findings.why: This is a flat cultural generalisation presented as fact, unlike the rest of the article, which consistently tags impressions as 'in our experience' or as unmeasured first-hand observation. It does not affect a safety decision, but it breaks the attribution discipline the piece otherwise maintains.
findings.fix: Mark it as observation — e.g. 'In our experience a specific, apologetic ask is usually met well' — matching the framing used elsewhere in the piece.

findings.quote: We are describing what has worked for us in Seoul and Gyeonggi as a couple managing NCGS.
findings.why: The evidence-base statement earlier in the body includes a third region ('across Seoul, Gyeonggi and Cheonan'), so the closing scope statement narrows the stated basis without explanation. A reader auditing the evidence base gets two different answers about where these observations come from.
findings.fix: Make the two scope statements identical — add Cheonan to the closing limits bullet, or drop it from the earlier one if the Cheonan observations are thinner.
